clue.text: Fish in box turned stiff

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the word for box is read backwards

parts.note: to box someone's ears is to clip them
stiff and hard both mean rigid

explanation.surface: A fish packed in a box has gone rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' as a container is the trap; it is the verb, to strike someone round the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilchard is a small oily sea fish of the herring family, often sold canned.

clue.text: One's found in better jam

indicators.note: being found in something means sitting inside it, so one word goes within another

parts.note: to better something is to improve it
one is I, and the 's is IS

explanation.surface: Someone discovered in a superior preserve, or a better musical jam session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jam' looks like the fruit preserve but is the musicians' verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To jam is to play music spontaneously, which is what improvising means.

clue.text: Where convict is beginning to train musician

parts.note: a convict is kept in a prison cell
taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of train

explanation.surface: Somewhere a prisoner is starting to learn to play music.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist is a musician who plays the cello.

clue.text: Tropical bird featured in a stamp?

parts.note: taken as written
British workers once had a National Insurance stamp, NI for short, fixed to a card each week

explanation.surface: An exotic bird pictured on a postage stamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a postage stamp; the question mark flags the older British sense of a National Insurance contribution stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: The ani is a black cuckoo of tropical America.

clue.text: Like everything, mostly computerised?

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it
it all is everything

explanation.surface: Is everything these days more or less run by computer?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a comparison but is the verb meaning to enjoy. The question mark admits that digital is only an example of computerised.
explanation.definitionFit: Digital technology is the kind computers use, so a computerised process can be called digital.

clue.text: Bob's insult on the cricket pitch

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bob or bobsleigh is a sled for snow

explanation.surface: A man called Bob insults someone during a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name but is the winter sled. Sledging is cricket slang for fielders verbally abusing the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a sled for snow and the cricketing practice of taunting opponents to break their concentration.

clue.text: This is small and it can clean lounge

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
taken as written
a can is a tin
to groom an animal is to clean it

explanation.surface: A small room that someone could easily clean.
explanation.definitionFit: A lounge and a sitting room are both the main living room where people relax.

clue.text: Migrant is not welcomed by each country

indicators.note: someone welcomed by a host is taken inside, so one piece goes within another
a migrant moves about, so these letters move to new places

parts.note: the first half of EA, the abbreviation for each
these letters rearranged
the second half of EA, the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: A migrant is turned away by every country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Migrant' looks like the subject but is the shuffle signal; the scrambled letters go inside EA, the abbreviation for each.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic country in northern Europe.

clue.text: Turn left perhaps to warn of attack

parts.note: to turn, as in turn cold, is to grow or become
L is the abbreviation for left, one of several things it can stand for

explanation.surface: Turning left as a signal that an attack is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn left' reads as a direction; it is two pieces, a verb meaning become and a one-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog growls as a low threatening sound that warns it may attack.

clue.text: Good way to cut use of fertiliser? It gets my vote!

indicators.note: a cut goes into something, so these letters are inserted into another word

parts.note: pollen fertilises plants, so its use is pollination
G is the abbreviation for good
ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A gardener backs a good method for reducing fertiliser use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It gets my vote!' sounds like enthusiastic approval but literally describes the place where a vote is cast.
explanation.definitionFit: A polling station is the building where voters cast their ballots, so it literally receives each vote.

clue.text: Now here's instant food

parts.note: a mo, short for moment, is an instant
a dish is a serving of food

explanation.surface: Here is some instant food available right now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now' is an adjective here, as in a now look: fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something now, in slang, is currently in fashion, which is what modish means.

clue.text: Ambassador refers to ceremonial attire

parts.note: an ambassador is addressed as His Excellency, abbreviated HE
to address a topic is to refer to it

explanation.surface: A diplomat mentions the formal dress code for an occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Headdresses are ornamental head coverings often worn as part of ceremonial costume.

clue.text: Shape integral to bust

indicators.note: something bust is broken, and its pieces can be put back in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A shape that is essential to a sculpted bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a sculpture or a chest but is the verb meaning break.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle is a three-sided geometric figure, an example of a shape.

clue.text: New parts have an effect on signal

indicators.note: a thing that parts opens up to let something in between its halves

parts.note: the first part of HIT; to hit is to have an effect
N is the abbreviation for new
the last part of HIT

explanation.surface: Fresh components influence a signal.
explanation.walkthrough: HIT parts to let N in. The word 'on' belongs to the surface phrase 'have an effect on' but only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hint is an indirect suggestion, a small signal of what someone means.

clue.text: Commitment for one in marriage

indicators.note: in places one item inside the word that follows

parts.note: the first part of ALLIANCE; a marriage is an alliance
e.g. means for example, for one
the rest of ALLIANCE

explanation.surface: Commitment is something one gives in marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegiance is loyal commitment to a cause, country or person.

clue.text: Catch a cold etc — catching one is great

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to cop is slang for to catch
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
the first two letters of etc
the Roman numeral for one
the last letter of etc

explanation.surface: Catching a cold and so on is supposedly wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: ETC catches I to give ETIC after COP, A and C. 'Catch a cold' reads as one phrase but splits into three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Copacetic is American slang meaning fine or excellent, everything in good order.

clue.text: Muscle, dodgy one, suffering with zip slip

parts.note: a pec is a pectoral muscle
a cad is a dishonourable man
someone ill is suffering
zip is nothing, zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A dodgy muscleman in pain catches himself in a zip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zip slip' tempts as a phrase about a fastener; zip is zero and slip stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A peccadillo is a small sin or fault, a minor slip in behaviour.

clue.text: Prisoner gets hammer inside piece of bread

indicators.note: inside places one word within the word around it

parts.note: the first letter of CON, a convict
to hammer an opponent is to rout them
the rest of CON

explanation.surface: An inmate smuggles a hammer inside a loaf, the old file-in-the-cake trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hammer' looks like the tool but is the verb, to beat soundly.
explanation.definitionFit: A crouton is a small cube of fried or toasted bread served on soup or salad.

clue.text: Slow PC network with short lead

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a LAN is a local area network linking computers
to lead someone is to guide them

explanation.surface: A sluggish computer network blamed on a short cable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like a cable, but it is the verb, to guide.
explanation.definitionFit: Languid means relaxed and unhurried, slow through lack of energy.

clue.text: The best place to turn

indicators.note: turning round makes the word face the other way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: a spot is a place

explanation.surface: The ideal place to make a turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Tops is informal for the very best, as in that film is the tops.

clue.text: Oiled nut, one securing a vintage car part

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is held inside another
oiled is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lubricated nut fixes something to a vintage car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oiled' looks mechanical, fitting nut and car, but it means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonneau is the rear passenger section of an early open car, or a cover over it.

clue.text: Christmas over, roast flipping pig

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: Noel is Christmas
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
to pan a show is to roast it, criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: Christmas is done, so it is time to roast a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roast' tempts as cooking the pig; it is harsh criticism. 'flipping' poses as a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon is the pig who becomes dictator in Orwell's Animal Farm.

clue.text: Crazy bridges over bypass

indicators.note: a bridge spans something, so one word straddles another

parts.note: the first part of AVID; crazy about something is avid for it
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
the rest of AVID

explanation.surface: Wild bridges built over a bypass road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bypass' looks like a road but is the verb, to skirt round.
explanation.definitionFit: To bypass something is to go round it, which is to avoid it.

clue.text: German city, one framed by artist

indicators.note: a picture framed by something is surrounded by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the start of MUNCH, the Norwegian painter of The Scream
the Roman numeral for one
the rest of MUNCH

explanation.surface: A German city where someone was set up by a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Munich is the capital of Bavaria in southern Germany.

clue.text: Central point of crossword?

indicators.note: central picks the middle of the word, keeping only its centre letters

parts.note: the three letters at the centre of crossword

explanation.surface: What is the central point of a crossword puzzle?
explanation.walkthrough: SSW is the standard abbreviation for south-south-west, written out in full in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: South-south-west is one of the sixteen named points of the compass.

clue.text: Not cock of the north

indicators.note: of here means taken from within, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Not the cock of the north, a phrase for a local champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cock of the north' reads as one phrase, so the split after 'Not cock' is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen is the female fowl, so it is the bird that is not a cock.

clue.text: A scholar is a lovely man

parts.note: taken as written
a don is a university lecturer
taken as written

explanation.surface: An academic who happens to be very handsome.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis, the beautiful youth of Greek myth, is used for any strikingly handsome man.

clue.text: Retreat's a little bit rubbish

parts.note: a den is a private retreat
an ounce is a small amount

explanation.surface: Someone's hideaway is a bit of a tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbish' looks like a noun but is the British verb meaning to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish something, in British slang, is to condemn it, which is to denounce it.
